bamboo-flooring-installation.q: How much does bamboo flooring installation cost in Australia?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Bamboo flooring installation in Australia typically costs $40–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on flooring grade and subfloor prep. Foam underlay adds around $14 per square metre. A 40m² room installation typically lands between $1,600 and $6,000 including materials and labour. Get a few quotes to compare like for like.

bamboo-flooring-installation.q: Is bamboo flooring a good option for Australian homes?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Bamboo flooring suits most Australian homes, offering hardwood looks at a lower price with good scratch resistance. It performs best in stable indoor climates since it can expand or contract with humidity swings, so coastal and tropical homes need acclimatised, quality-grade boards. Avoid areas with standing water like bathrooms and laundries.

bamboo-flooring-installation.q: Does bamboo flooring need an underlay?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Yes, bamboo flooring should go over a foam underlay, which costs around $14 per square metre at Bunnings. Underlay cushions the boards, reduces footstep noise, and evens out minor subfloor imperfections. On concrete slabs a moisture barrier layer is also recommended before laying, since bamboo is sensitive to rising damp.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: How much does ceiling insulation installation cost in Australia?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Ceiling insulation installation in Australia costs $10–$25 per square metre supply and install. R4.0 batts run $61–$124 a pack at Bunnings, with coverage varying by product thickness. For an average 150m² home this typically totals $1,500–$3,750 for a full ceiling cavity installed by a licensed installer.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: What R-value ceiling insulation is recommended in Australia?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Most Australian homes use R4.0 batts in the ceiling, which suit most climate zones for comfortable year-round performance. Cooler regions typically benefit from a higher R-value, while warmer northern areas can get by with slightly less. A qualified insulation installer can confirm the right rating for your roof space and location before you buy.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: How long does ceiling insulation take to install?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Ceiling insulation installation typically takes half a day to a full day for an average home, depending on roof access and cavity size. Installers lay batts between and over the ceiling joists from inside the roof space. Homes with restricted roof access or existing insulation needing removal can take longer.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: How much does a concrete retaining wall cost in Australia?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: A concrete retaining wall in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on wall height, reinforcement, and site access. Reinforcing bar and formwork add to material costs, and drainage behind the wall is essential. A modest 10m² wall usually falls between $500 and $1,500.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: Does a concrete retaining wall need drainage?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: Yes, every concrete retaining wall needs drainage behind it to relieve water pressure that can crack or push over the wall. Standard practice uses slotted ag pipe wrapped in drainage gravel, running along the base and out to a discharge point. Skipping drainage is one of the most common causes of retaining wall failure.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: How thick should a concrete retaining wall be?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: Wall thickness depends on height and the soil load behind it, but most residential concrete retaining walls under one metre use around 150–200mm of reinforced concrete. Taller walls need thicker sections, deeper footings, and engineered reinforcement with N12 bar. Always get a structural design for anything retaining significant soil height.

epoxy-flooring.q: How much does epoxy flooring cost in Australia?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy flooring in Australia costs $40–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on the number of coats and surface prep needed. A DIY epoxy coating kit runs $53–$198 at Bunnings, cheaper but harder to get a durable finish. Professional installers grind and prime the concrete first for proper adhesion.

epoxy-flooring.q: What are the downsides of epoxy flooring?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy flooring can be slippery when wet unless an anti-slip additive is mixed in, and it shows scratches and yellowing over time with UV exposure. It also needs a well-prepped, dry concrete slab, since moisture underneath causes bubbling and peeling. Repairs mean patching or recoating rather than simple spot fixes.

epoxy-flooring.q: What surfaces can epoxy flooring not be applied to?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy will not bond well to sealed or waxed concrete, damp slabs, or flexible surfaces like vinyl and some timber, since it needs a porous, mechanically ground surface to key into. It also struggles on surfaces contaminated with oil or grease. A professional will grind and test the slab before quoting a job.

french-drain-installation.q: How much does a French drain cost to install in Australia?
french-drain-installation.a: A French drain installation in Australia typically costs $300–$2,000 per job, depending on length, depth, and ground conditions. Materials like slotted ag pipe and drainage gravel are inexpensive, so most of the cost is labour for digging the trench and correctly grading the fall. Longer runs across a whole yard sit at the higher end.

french-drain-installation.q: What is a French drain used for?
french-drain-installation.a: A French drain is a gravel-filled trench with a slotted or perforated pipe underneath that redirects groundwater away from a house, retaining wall, or waterlogged garden bed. It works by letting water seep through the gravel into the pipe, then carries it to a discharge point or stormwater connection. It is a common fix for soggy yards and damp foundations.

french-drain-installation.q: How deep should a French drain be?
french-drain-installation.a: Most residential French drains sit around 300 to 600mm deep, enough to intercept groundwater above the footing line without undermining it. Depth also depends on what the drain is protecting, with retaining walls often needing a deeper trench than a simple garden drainage line. A tradesperson will grade the trench with a slight fall toward the outlet.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace a hot water system in Australia?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: Replacing a hot water system in Australia typically costs $80–$200 per hour in plumber labour, plus the unit itself. An electric storage hot water system costs $98–$528 depending on tank size and brand, so a straightforward swap often lands between $600 and $1,500 including installation. Gas or heat pump units cost more upfront.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How long does a hot water system last?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: Most electric storage hot water systems last around 8 to 12 years, while gas and heat pump units can run a bit longer with regular servicing. Signs it needs replacing include rusty water, rumbling noises, or leaks around the base of the tank. Replacing before a full failure avoids water damage and an unplanned cold shower.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How long does it take to replace a hot water system?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: A straightforward like-for-like hot water system replacement usually takes a licensed plumber 2 to 4 hours, including draining the old tank and connecting the new one. Switching between fuel types, such as electric to gas, takes longer due to extra pipework and compliance checks. Most homes are back to hot water the same day.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: How much does a kitchen splashback cost to tile in Australia?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: A tiled kitchen splashback in Australia typically costs $45–$120 per square metre supply and install. Ceramic wall tiles run $14–$59 per square metre, plus adhesive and grout, so a standard 3 to 4 square metre splashback often totals $200–$500 in materials before labour. Mosaic or feature tiles push the price toward the higher end.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: What is the best tile for a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: Ceramic and porcelain tiles are the most popular kitchen splashback choice in Australia, since they resist heat, grease, and staining while being easy to wipe clean. Glass and mosaic tiles suit a feature look but cost more and can be trickier to grout cleanly around powerpoints and rangehoods. Gloss finishes brighten a kitchen and make cleaning easier.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: How long does it take to tile a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: Tiling a standard kitchen splashback usually takes a tiler one day, covering measuring, cutting around powerpoints, laying tiles, and grouting once the adhesive has set. Larger or more intricate patterns, like herringbone or mosaic, can take an extra day. Allow another day before the grout fully cures if you plan to use the stovetop straight away.

paving-and-pathways.q: How much does paving cost per square metre in Australia?
paving-and-pathways.a: Paving in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on paver type and base preparation. Concrete pavers cost around $15 each at Bunnings, with paving sand and crusher dust adding to the base cost. A basic 20m² pathway usually runs $1,000–$3,000 including labour.

paving-and-pathways.q: What is the cheapest type of paving?
paving-and-pathways.a: Concrete pavers are generally the cheapest paving option in Australia, costing around $15 each compared with natural stone options like bluestone or travertine, which run well above $100 per square metre. Crushed gravel or crusher dust paths cost even less but are not as durable or level underfoot. Concrete still gives a clean, long-lasting finish for the price.

Laying pavers yourself is possible for a small, flat area like a garden path, but getting the base compacted and level takes practice. Professional pavers excavate, compact a road base or crusher dust layer, then bed pavers in sand with consistent joints and fall for drainage. Skipping proper base prep is the main reason DIY paving sinks or cracks later.

render-repair.q: How much does render repair cost in Australia?
render-repair.a: Render repair in Australia typically costs $30–$80 per square metre, covering crack filling, patching, and reblending the finish to match existing render. Polymer render mix costs around $15 per 20kg bag at Bunnings for small DIY patches. Larger areas of cracking or delamination cost more, since loose render often needs to be hacked off before repair.

Render cracks mainly from movement in the building, moisture getting behind the render, or render that was applied too thick or over a poorly prepared surface. Hairline cracks are usually cosmetic, but wider or spreading cracks can let water in and damage the wall behind. Fixing the underlying cause matters as much as patching the crack itself.

render-repair.q: Can you patch render or does the whole wall need redoing?
render-repair.a: Small cracks and localised damage can usually be patched without redoing the whole wall, provided the surrounding render is sound and well bonded. If render is bulging, hollow-sounding when tapped, or crumbling over a large area, it usually needs to be removed and reapplied in that section. A tradesperson can tell the difference with a simple tap test.

sewer-line-replacement.q: How much does sewer line replacement cost in Australia?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Sewer line replacement in Australia typically costs $80–$200 per hour in plumber labour, with the total heavily dependent on pipe length, depth, and whether trenchless relining is used instead of full excavation. PVC pipe itself is cheap at $6–$32 per length, so labour and access dominate the final price.

sewer-line-replacement.q: What are the signs a sewer line needs replacing?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Common signs include recurring blockages, gurgling drains, sewage smells in the yard, wet or sunken patches over the pipe run, and toilets that drain slowly despite clearing. Tree root intrusion and old clay or earthenware pipes are frequent culprits in older homes. A camera inspection confirms whether the line needs relining or full replacement.

sewer-line-replacement.q: Do I need to dig up my yard to replace a sewer line?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Not always. Trenchless relining can rehabilitate a damaged sewer pipe through small access points, avoiding a full dig-up in many cases. It works best on pipes that are cracked or root-affected but still structurally intact. Severely collapsed or misaligned sections usually still need traditional excavation to replace the pipe properly.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: How much does stormwater drainage installation cost in Australia?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Stormwater drainage installation in Australia typically costs $300–$2,000 per job, depending on pipe length, number of pits, and how much excavation is needed. A grated drainage pit costs $41–$108 each, with PVC stormwater pipe adding $6–$26 per length. Connecting into council stormwater infrastructure or dealing with tree roots can push costs higher.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: What is the difference between stormwater and regular drainage?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Stormwater drainage specifically manages rainwater runoff from roofs, driveways, and paved areas, carrying it away through pipes and pits to the street system or a legal point of discharge. General site drainage, like a French drain, deals with groundwater or subsurface moisture around footings and gardens. The two systems often connect but serve different jobs.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: Why is proper stormwater drainage important?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Poor stormwater drainage lets water pool against foundations, erode garden beds, and flood low points in the yard during heavy rain, which over time can cause structural and damp problems. A properly graded system with pits and piped connections moves runoff away from the house to a legal discharge point, protecting the property long term.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a wall-hung vanity in Australia?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: A wall-hung vanity unit costs $451–$1,999 in Australia, with $1,102 typical for a quality 900mm unit, plus $93–$326 for a basin mixer tap. Installed as a standalone swap by a plumber, labour typically adds a few hundred dollars on top. As part of a full bathroom renovation, overall project costs commonly run from $15,000–$35,000.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: Why choose a wall-hung vanity over a floor-standing one?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: A wall-hung vanity makes a small bathroom feel larger by leaving the floor visible underneath, and it makes mopping and cleaning easier since there is nothing blocking the skirting. It also suits modern, minimalist bathroom designs. The trade-off is it needs solid wall reinforcement, since the cabinet and any stored items hang entirely off brackets fixed into the studs.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: Does a wall need extra support for a wall-hung vanity?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: Yes, a wall-hung vanity needs solid backing, usually a plywood or timber noggin fitted between the wall studs, to carry the weight of the cabinet, benchtop, and basin. Standard plasterboard alone will not hold the brackets long term. This backing is normally installed during a renovation before the wall is sheeted and tiled, so it pays to plan ahead.
